articles.title: Payday to mayday: The hike mirage and why bigger salaries still feel smaller
articles.summary: Aamdani atthanni, kharcha rupaiya! It is a familiar refrain, and a financial loop the common man spends a lifetime trying to escape.
articles.body: Aamdani atthanni, kharcha rupaiya!It is a familiar refrain, and a financial loop the common man spends a lifetime trying to escape.For India's middle class, much of working life revolves around one big aspiration: earning enough to afford not just the essentials, but also the little pleasures and milestones that make the grind worthwhile.A bigger paycheque promises more than a fatter bank balance. It means the freedom to make that impulsive purchase, finally book that long-awaited holiday, put money into an investment or simply save a little more towards a secure future.Yet, the closer that promise seems, the more elusive it becomes. Because every salary hike brings with it a familiar question: how much of that extra money will actually stay?For many Indian households, annual increments are increasingly being eaten up by rising everyday expenses, leaving little room to feel richer, save more or get ahead financially.Companies are offering average salary hikes of around 9%, yet households are reporting higher spending on essentials, rising financial commitments and declining confidence about the economy.The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) September 2026 survey found that 90.1% of urban households were spending more on essentials than a year ago. Meanwhile, 54.5% felt the economic situation had worsened, compared with 40.9% in September 2025.The problem, therefore, is not simply how much people earn, but how much of that income survives after paying for necessities and accounting for inflation.With food prices climbing, fuel costs adding to the burden and household borrowing increasing, a rising pay packet does not necessarily mean a bigger financial cushion.Jyoti Prakash Gadia, managing director of Resurgent India Limited, said that the rising cost of basic necessities was eating into the disposable income generated by salary increases. Housing, healthcare, education, transport, EMIs and insurance premiums were claiming a larger share of household budgets, limiting the improvement in purchasing power."Although there has been some growth in household income levels, the increasing cost of basic necessities has placed pressure on the disposable income levels," Gadia said.Attractive hikes on paperFor someone working a corporate job, appraisal season often brings a glimmer of hope and, over the past few years, salary hikes have given employees some reason to look forward to it.A recent Aon's salary survey found that companies offered an average hike of 9% in 2026 and expect to increase salaries by 9.1% in 2027.Deloitte's survey of India Inc. also projected an average increment of around 9.1%.At first glance, that sounds like exactly what every 9-to-5 employee waits and works for. But by the time those numbers translate into actual money in the bank, the excitement can begin to fade.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();For instance, with September's retail inflation standing above 5%, a 9% salary hike translates into an approximate 3.3% gain in real terms, based on the headline inflation figure. However, the actual benefit can look quite different once taxes, deductions and individual spending patterns enter the picture.Government labour data paints a more uneven picture.According to the ministry of statistics and programme implementation's (MoSPI) latest Periodic Labour Force Survey for 2025, average monthly earnings of regular salaried men increased by 5.8%, from Rs 22,891 to Rs 24,217. For women, the increase was 7.2%, from Rs 17,126 to Rs 18,353. Self-employed men recorded a wage increase of around 6%.For casual workers, however, the numbers offer little reason to celebrate. Average daily wages for male casual labourers remained virtually unchanged at Rs 455, compared with Rs 456 earlier.When salaries stay the same but grocery bills, travel costs and other expenses keep rising, making it through the month itself can become a challenge.Gadia said that the gap between income growth and the cost of living was particularly difficult for households with large fixed commitments. Even when salaries increased, rising EMIs, insurance premiums and other recurring payments could leave families with little additional disposable income.Food prices take a bigger biteThe biggest source of pressure is increasingly visible in grocery bills. Retail inflation climbed to 5.54% in September this year, its highest level under the new Consumer Price Index (CPI) series.This was also the fourth consecutive month that inflation remained above the RBI's 4% target.Food inflation rose sharply to 7.74% in September from 5.97% in August. Some everyday kitchen essentials became considerably more expensive, with onion prices increasing 108% year on year, ginger becoming 63% costlier and garlic prices rising 55%.The pressure has been particularly pronounced in rural India.Rural inflation stood at 6.08%, compared with 4.88% in urban areas, while rural food inflation reached 8.06%.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The weather has added to the challenge.The India Meteorological Department reported that the 2026 monsoon ended at 87% of the long-period average, its weakest performance since 2015. The possibility of El Niño conditions peaking in November has also added uncertainty to the agricultural outlook.The government's foodgrain production target for 2026-27 stands at 373.93 million tonnes, lower than the 376.56 million tonnes recorded in the previous year.For households, the impact is difficult to avoid. People can postpone buying a new phone, cut down on restaurant visits or cancel a holiday, but groceries remain a monthly necessity.Gadia said families were increasingly prioritising basic needs and becoming more selective about discretionary purchases. Higher rent, tuition fees, medical expenses and utility bills were leaving households with fewer options to adjust their budgets."Today, families find themselves having tighter household budgets due to the rising expenses in basic necessities like accommodation, education, health care, food and transport," he said.He added that households were increasingly opting for bargain shopping, delaying non-essential purchases and cutting back on entertainment, travel and lifestyle expenses to keep their finances stable.Why your monthly budget just doesn't add upThere is another reason households may feel more pressure than the headline inflation figure suggests: everyone's spending basket is different.MoSPI's Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) for 2023-24 found that food accounted for 47.04% of household spending in rural India and 39.68% in urban areas.Average monthly per capita consumption expenditure stood at Rs 4,122 in rural India and Rs 6,996 in urban India.When food inflation rises to 7.74%, households that devote a larger share of their income to groceries naturally feel a greater squeeze.The new CPI series has also reduced the weight assigned to food and beverages from 45.86% to 36.75%, reflecting changes in household consumption patterns.This means food price increases have a smaller influence on the headline inflation number than they did under the previous series.Not every expense, however, is rising at the same pace. September data showed inflation in housing and fuel at 2.74%, education at 3.94% and healthcare at 1.40%. Food and beverages recorded inflation of 7.36% under the category-wise CPI classification, while restaurants and accommodation saw a sharper increase of 9.36%.This is why two families earning identical salaries can have very different experiences.A household paying rent, school fees and home loan instalments may have considerably less flexibility than one with fewer fixed commitments.There is also a difference between inflation slowing and prices actually falling. Even if inflation comes down, it only means prices are increasing at a slower rate. It does not reverse the price increases households have already absorbed.Gadia pointed out that housing, education and healthcare costs could continue to rise faster than a family's income even when overall inflation appeared to be under control. This can erode the advantage of salary increments, particularly for households whose earnings growth is low or unpredictable.Household confidence is slipping despite higher incomesThe gap between official inflation and what people experience is also reflected in RBI's consumer surveys.In September, households reported median perceived inflation of 8.4% and expected it to reach 10% over the next year.This is considerably higher than the official retail inflation rate of 5.54%.Interestingly, the difference between the two has narrowed over the past year.In September 2025, households perceived inflation at 7.4%, even when official CPI inflation was just 1.44%. While perceived inflation has increased by around one percentage point since then, official inflation has climbed by approximately four percentage points.Consumer confidence has also weakened.The RBI's urban current situation index fell from 96.9 in September 2025 to 87.9 in September 2026. Its rural counterpart declined from 100.9 to 90.6.A reading below 100 indicates that more households view economic conditions as worsening than improving.The difference between essential and discretionary spending is particularly telling. Among urban households, the net response on spending on essentials stood at 88.4, while the corresponding reading for non-essential purchases was just 4.6.In simple terms, households are continuing to spend where they have little choice, but are becoming far more cautious about everything else.Gadia told TOI that this change was visible in the way families were approaching their monthly budgets. They were cutting back on discretionary spending, postponing large purchases and turning to less expensive alternatives. Regular expenses, including subscriptions and consumer credit payments, were also becoming part of the household budget calculations.Rising oil prices could make the squeeze worseFood is not the only expense putting pressure on household budgets. Fuel prices have added another layer of uncertainty.The US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28, has kept crude oil prices elevated. Petrol and diesel prices were increased by Rs 3 per litre on May 15, marking their first hike in nearly four years.Union oil minister Hardeep Singh Puri said state-run refiners were incurring losses of around Rs 10 billion a day while keeping retail fuel prices low.The pressure is not limited to petrol and diesel bills. Higher crude prices can increase transportation, manufacturing and distribution costs, eventually feeding into the prices of goods and services.Wholesale inflation offers an indication of these pressures. It rose to 11.39% in September, almost double the retail inflation rate.Fuel and power prices increased 25.85%, while manufactured goods inflation reached 9.76%.However, higher wholesale inflation does not automatically translate into an equivalent increase in retail prices. Businesses may initially absorb some of the additional costs, depending on their margins, competition and demand. If these pressures persist, they could eventually pass on part of the burden to consumers.RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra has cautioned that "inflation and its outlook are not benign, as they were last year".The central bank expects headline inflation to average nearly 5.8% over the next three quarters.At the same time, a depreciating rupee could add to the problem by making imported inputs more expensive.Households are borrowing more, but are they saving enough?When monthly expenses begin to outpace income growth, borrowing can become a convenient way to bridge a gap. But loans also bring another fixed expense into an already stretched household budget.RBI data show that household debt increased to 45.9% of GDP in March 2026, compared with 36.4% in June 2022. During this period, household debt increased 78%, while financial assets grew 49%.In 2025-26, households added Rs 42.9 lakh crore to their financial assets but also took on Rs 21.4 lakh crore in fresh loans. Net financial savings declined to 6.2% of GDP from 7% earlier.The composition of borrowing is another concern.Those families who have large EMI or low emergency funds are at particular risk in case of any financial shocks. Regular savings impact retirement plans in the future.According to the RBI's Financial Stability Report, non-housing retail loans, including personal loans, credit card debt and gold loans, account for 58.4% of household debt.Delinquencies in small-ticket loans increased to 6.4% in March 2026.Higher interest rates could make repayments more expensive. For instance, assuming a full pass-through, a 0.25 percentage point increase in the interest rate on a Rs 50 lakh home loan with a 20-year tenure, initially priced at 8.5%, would raise the monthly EMI from approximately Rs 43,391 to Rs 44,186.That is an additional Rs 794 every month.For a household already juggling groceries, school fees, rent and other bills, even a seemingly small increase can make a difference.Gadia cautioned that households relying on credit cards, personal loans and long repayment plans to meet short-term financial needs could find themselves under greater pressure over time. While borrowing may offer temporary relief, interest costs can add to the burden and reduce the money available for savings.He also noted that families facing higher expenses may cut back on discretionary savings or dip into existing reserves. Such adjustments may help in the short term, but can affect longer-term financial goals, including retirement planning.The pressure is particularly acute for households with large EMIs or inadequate emergency funds, which may have limited capacity to absorb an unexpected financial shock.The expert told TOI, "Having an emergency fund that consists of enough money to last for up to six months of living costs is also vital. Households need to reduce unnecessary borrowing, assess their insurance and make steady investments according to their goals and risk tolerance. Diversifying their savings in appropriate financial instruments may also assist them in mitigating risks."Will your next salary hike be enough?The coming months will offer a clearer picture of whether income growth can withstand the renewed inflationary pressure.With wholesale inflation running significantly higher than retail inflation, the possibility of businesses passing on additional costs remains a concern. If retail inflation moves towards the RBI's projected average of 5.8%, the real benefit of a 9% salary increase could shrink to around 3.2%, based on a simple comparison of the two figures.Against the 8.4% inflation households currently perceive, however, the difference falls to just 0.6 percentage points. This is an illustrative calculation, rather than a measure of actual household purchasing power.The next retail inflation reading is scheduled for November 12, followed by wholesale inflation data on November 16.The RBI's next monetary policy meeting is scheduled for December 2-4.A household must develop a systematic way of handling its finances through regular assessments of its income, expenditure, liabilities and savings obligations. Budgeting for oneself realistically and focusing on necessary spending and cutting out unnecessary monthly expenses can help one be more financially flexible.For households, the bigger question is whether their earnings can keep pace with the rising cost of necessities without forcing them to borrow more or cut back on savings. For businesses, it is whether higher input costs can be passed on to customers who are already becoming cautious about discretionary spending.For individuals, Gadia recommends a more systematic approach to managing household finances. This includes regularly reviewing income, expenses, liabilities and savings commitments, identifying avoidable monthly costs and ensuring that investments are aligned with financial goals and risk tolerance.He also recommends maintaining an emergency fund capable of covering up to six months of living expenses, while reviewing insurance coverage and avoiding unnecessary borrowing.Ultimately, a salary hike is only one part of the financial picture. What matters is how much money remains after the monthly bills are paid, loan instalments are cleared and essential purchases are made.Because a bigger pay packet may look good on paper, but the real raise is what helps you escape the ‘mehengai ki maar!’You use AI every day. articles.title: Why Trump’s favorite CNN video of Harry Enten is ‘not the full story’
articles.summary: CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten has become an unexpected star at President Donald Trump’s rallies this fall.
articles.body: CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten has become an unexpected star at President Donald Trump’s rallies this fall. In state after state, Trump has shown a montage of Enten’s appearances on CNN, highlighting moments when Enten has highlighted the president’s enduring popularity among self-professed MAGA Republicans. The CNN video clips have been played at rallies at least 16 times during this month’s midterm blitz. Trump often stands and watches the clips on a giant screen while rallygoers cheer Enten’s remarks. Sometimes Trump says “wow” or “thank you, CNN” after the montage is played. But the clips are devoid of any context and can easily leave viewers with a misimpression of Trump’s real political standing. So I asked Enten about the montage and its relevance to the impending midterm election. Our conversation has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Stelter: You’re the data guy, so let’s start with some numbers: Roughly how many TV segments and videos have you made about the midterms this year? Enten: Oh my… well, let’s think about this… There have been over 300 days in 2026 so far… I am on TV pretty much every day, including weekends. I’ve taken off some time… but I think 300 segments is a fair starting point. It may be more! Maybe much more, but let’s play it conservatively. Stelter: Clearly the president has been watching some of those segments. Last year, he name-checked you but butchered your name. This year, he’s been pronouncing it correctly. He likes to say “even CNN” is reporting something flattering about him, and then he’ll invoke you. Is that surreal for you? Enten: Well, if you had told me a decade ago that I would a) be on CNN, and b) the president of the United States would be playing clips of mine at his rallies… I don’t think I would have bought it for a minute. I’d put the chance at 1 in a million… and that may have been high. Stelter: So about those clips: Why does he keep playing them? Enten: Because he believes it shows him to be popular. The Trump brand is all about winning, and those clips, in his mind, show him winning. Stelter: What are you saying in the clips? Enten: Well, I believe there are two clips he plays… Maybe three. Gotta be honest, I spend my free time watching episodes of “Blossom.” But one, I think, is a clip about how approval with MAGA is basically matching his support he received from them in 2024. Another is support for GOP House candidates is basically matching Trump’s support from 2024. The third is how, among the GOP, he is by far the most admired president. He beats out Reagan and Lincoln. Stelter: Everything you said in those clips was true at the time, of course. But is some of the info outdated at this point? Enten: I haven’t seen another “most admired” poll, but I bet Trump still leads that handily. He’s slightly lower with the MAGA GOP than he was, but the MAGA GOP support for congressional GOP candidates is the same, if not a little higher. That is per Fox News polling. Of course, MAGA GOP is just a portion of the electorate. Stelter: That’s really the key, right? Trump keeps conflating “MAGA Republicans” with all Republicans. What proportion of Republicans don’t ID as MAGA? Enten: It depends on the poll. But I think it’s safe to say a sizable minority do not identify as MAGA. Among non-MAGA GOP, Trump is actually underwater in some polls. Stelter: Is “MAGA Republican” even a useful category? Isn’t it just like measuring Trump’s approval rating? Enten: Want to know the story about why I started pulling the metric? Stelter: Yes! Enten: So the reason, as I recall, was that in the early days of the Iran War, there was all this talk about how MAGA was infighting because of the war. This got me thinking, “Is this actually true?” There really wasn’t. MAGA is a self-defined category, right? But the people who were opting in loved Trump. I think it’s useful insofar as helping us understand MAGA essentially equals Trump. If that ever changes, it would be interesting. Stelter: Agreed. Now you’re on TV every day previewing the midterms, talking about many other metrics. Trump doesn’t promote those segments for obvious reasons: You’re showing that his party is in big trouble, electorally speaking. Does that have a lot to do with MAGA GOP versus non-MAGA GOP? Enten: There are two reasons the GOP is in major trouble. The first is what you pointed out about non-MAGA GOP. James Talarico, for example, is getting a substantial portion of that vote in Texas. The second is independents. Trump’s the least popular president going into a midterm on record with independents. He’s even less popular than Nixon was before he was forced out in August of 1974. Democrats for Congress are rolling with independents. They may put up their best margin with them in any election in the exit poll era — i.e., nearly 50 years of congressional exit polls. Stelter: We both know why Trump isn’t airing clips of you saying that at his rallies. But do you think he’s misleading rallygoers by cherry-picking some of your points about his base support? Enten: Here’s what I’ll say: I think you can watch my segments, short and long. The MAGA GOP is just a small part of them. They help tell a story, but it’s not the full story.

articles.title: Hello Kitty's spy drama lands in hot water: What went wrong with Sanrio in China
articles.summary: Hello Kitty maker Sanrio has come under fire in China over its collaboration with Japanese TV drama VIVANT.
articles.body: Hello Kitty maker Sanrio has come under fire in China over its collaboration with Japanese TV drama VIVANT.The partnership involved a range of soft toys, including Hello Kitty and other characters dressed as spies from the show. However, its storyline, which depicts a fictional Chinese intelligence agency capturing and torturing Japanese spies, upset Chinese audiences.Criticism grew on social media over several days, with Chinese state media also speaking out against the collaboration. Sanrio's Chinese subsidiary eventually announced that it was ending the partnership and all related promotional activities.The incident highlights the challenges foreign companies face in China's lucrative market, where brand associations and public statements can trigger strong reactions. French football star Kylian Mbappe recently faced a similar backlash after remarks about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong prompted several Chinese sponsors to cut ties with him.What was the Sanrio-VIVANT collaboration?VIVANT is a Japanese television drama produced by broadcaster TBS and also available on Netflix. The show revolves around Japanese spies and a terrorist organisation called Tent.Its latest season, which is currently being aired, features a fictional Chinese intelligence agency capturing and torturing some of the Japanese spies. This storyline became a point of contention among Chinese audiences following Sanrio's merchandise collaboration.Sanrio's Chinese subsidiary apologised for the controversy and said the partnership did not align with the group's corporate philosophy."We deeply apologize for the concern this has caused everyone," Sanrio's Chinese subsidiary said in a statement."Regarding this collaboration, we believe it contains expressions that are inconsistent with the corporate philosophy of the Sanrio Group. We have therefore decided to terminate this collaboration along with all subsequent projects and promotional activities."TBS did not immediately comment on the cancellation.TBS President Masamine Ryuho said at a regular press conference on Wednesday that the drama is "entirely fictional and has no intention of disparaging any specific country", local media reported.Why are Japanese companies facing challenges in China?The controversy comes amid strained relations between China and Japan.Tensions increased after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said late last year that a hypothetical Chinese attack on democratically ruled Taiwan could trigger a military response from Tokyo.China has since urged its citizens not to travel to Japan and throttled exports of rare earths to the country. These minerals are important for manufacturing products ranging from cars to weapons.Despite the tensions, Japanese companies, including Sanrio, continue to rely on China for sales.Sanrio recorded sales of 9.8 billion yen ($62 million) in China in the first quarter, almost 25% higher than in the same period a year earlier.Several international companies have faced criticism in China over advertisements and comments. In 2018, Dolce & Gabbana cancelled a fashion show in Shanghai after advertisements showed a Chinese woman struggling to eat pizza and spaghetti with chopsticks.In 2021, H&M, Nike and Adidas also faced criticism over comments about labour conditions in Xinjiang. The recent incidents involving Sanrio and Mbappe are further examples of the challenges foreign companies and celebrities face while operating in the Chinese market.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Reason why NDA govt wins people's trust': Sitharaman hails World Bank's 6 key findings on India's poverty reduction
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Friday cited the World Bank's October 2026 Poverty and Equity Brief, saying India had recorded one of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Friday cited the World Bank's October 2026 Poverty and Equity Brief, saying India had recorded one of the fastest declines in poverty globally.She also credited the government's policies under Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the progress, saying it was the reason the NDA continued to enjoy people's trust and mandate.In a post on X, Sitharaman highlighted six key findings from the report, covering poverty reduction, employment growth, women's participation in the workforce, improvements in household welfare and access to electricity.Sharing the findings, Sitharaman said, "The World Bank’s October 2026 Poverty & Equity Brief records India’s progress as one of the fastest poverty declines in the world."The six key findings highlighted by the finance minister were:Poverty reduction: 49.6 crore people moved above the lower-middle-income poverty line of $4.20 a day between 2011 and 2023, with the poverty rate declining from 57.7% to 16.1%.Decline in extreme poverty: Extreme poverty declined from 27.1% to 2.6% over the same period, measured at $3 a day. Both monetary poverty thresholds use 2021 purchasing power parity.Employment growth: Employment increased by 13.4 crore people between 2017 and 2023, nearly twice the increase in the working-age population.Women's participation: Rural women accounted for a significant share of the employment gains, entering paid work and increasing the number of earners in their households.Improved household welfare: Both rural and urban households experienced substantial welfare gains, with faster progress in rural India narrowing the rural–urban gap.Electricity access: Access to electricity reached 99% of the population, according to the report's 2022 survey data.Sitharaman said the World Bank had identified strong consumption growth, rising employment, particularly among women, and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies, as key drivers of India's progress.She added that the government would continue to focus on productive employment, stronger household incomes and effective delivery of public services to build on the gains.The minister's remarks on poverty reduction came amid a political exchange with Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over the proposed sale of the government's stake in IDBI Bank to Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings.Rahul has opposed the disinvestment, arguing that public sector banks serve a larger purpose beyond commercial returns. In a letter to IDBI Bank employees on Thursday, he said the bank had turned around its financial performance and questioned the decision to sell it to a private investor."Seven years ago, IDBI was losing money. Last year, it earned a profit of over nine thousand crore rupees. That turnaround is your work," Rahul said in the letter.He added, "The Congress has always believed in a strong public sector working alongside the private sector. Public banks are not assets to be sold off, they are tools to build the nation."Rahul also raised concerns about the impact of the sale on employees' service conditions and reservations for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.Responding to his remarks, Sitharaman accused the Congress-led government of using banks and financial institutions as "personal entities" and pressuring them to extend loans without following prudent lending practices."IDBI Bank was handed over to us in poor shape, as IDBI itself was forced to lend to large business groups with close connections to @INCIndia leaders such as Videocon, Winsome, ABG Shipyard, and Kingfisher," Sitharaman earlier posted on social media."The NDA govt led by Hon'ble PM Shri @narendramodi revived the IDBI Bank through professionalism, prudence and recapitalisation of more than Rs 25,000 crores. The IDBI Bank is now poised for its next phase of growth," she added.The government on October 14 approved the sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax Financial Holdings for about Rs 53,000 crore ($5.5 billion).The transaction is expected to be completed by the end of the current financial year, subject to regulatory clearances from the Reserve Bank of India.The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) said on Thursday that the second round of bidding had been conducted under a procedure determined by the Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment, which was empowered by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs to address procedural issues and deviations.The clarification followed questions from various quarters, including the bank union, over the valuation of IDBI Bank and the bid price offered by Fairfax.You use AI every day. articles.title: Binance says user funds are safe after thieves make off with billions in largest-ever crypto hack
articles.summary: A record-setting cyberattack targeting the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has rocked the digital assets industry.
articles.body: A record-setting cyberattack targeting the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange rocked the digital assets industry Friday, delivering another blow to a sector already struggling to achieve mainstream adoption. The exchange, Binance, announced late Thursday that more than $6 billion appeared to have moved through wallets connected to a security breach. Around $3 billion of that had potentially been located and frozen across several exchanges, though it was not immediately clear if those funds were recoverable. It did not appear that the hackers were able to access customer accounts or holdings. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng released a video statement Friday morning that sought to reassure platform users. “Your assets are safe,” he said, adding “we never use customer funds, so they are not impacted.” Instead, Binance’s corporate holdings were affected, he said. The company said it had set aside $5 billion to cover the losses and was working with partners to purchase an additional $1.34 billion in cryptocurrencies to cover the total amount believed to have been stolen. In a statement, the Secret Service said it was working with private-sector partners, including U.S.-based crypto group Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance. It also said it was coordinating with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia and other law enforcement partners to identify those responsible. It said its investigation remained in early stages. The hack is the latest setback for crypto, which continues to reckon with a reputation for being too volatile — and too vulnerable to criminal activity — for widespread use. The scale of the hack echoes collapse of crypto exchange FTX, which, though not the result of a cyberattack, caused billions in losses. The renewed doubts were reflected in Bitcoin’s value Friday, which fell more than 5% overnight to approximately $77,000, accelerating its month-long downturn. Other affected cryptocurrencies fell as much as 9%. The crypto industry was already reeling from the failure in Congress of the Clarity Act, a bill that would have granted comprehensive legal protections for crypto assets in the U.S. Despite bipartisan support for the core elements of the legislation, its passage was torpedoed by a battle over conflict-of-interest rules for elected officials, notably President Donald Trump. The president has disclosed in filings that he earned more than $1 billion from crypto last year. The Binance hack stands to prolong this reckoning, experts said. “There will be an imperative for Binance to cover losses not only for its own reputation and value, but I expect there will be a level of co-operation within the space as they look at the collective reputational harm this may, rightly or wrongly, cause to the sector,” Laura Clatworthy, head of digital assets at the law firm Edwin Coe, said in a statement. That cooperation was seen in the immediate reaction of other mainstream crypto players. Crypto firms Tether and Circle, which operate the two-largest stablecoins, worked quickly to freeze assets implicated in the hack. However, U.S. blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs estimates that $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum will never be recovered. As of Friday morning, the hack’s origins remained murky. The whole heist unfolded in just 20 minutes starting at approximately 4 p.m. ET Thursday. Binance initially said the attack involved a compromised laptop. “However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” ‌it said in a statement on X, without elaborating. Multiple blockchain analysis firms said the hack had attributes associated with previous operations believed to have been carried out by North Korean actors. Teng, the Binance co-CEO, said Binance’s investigation had not yet identified the attackers. At least one prominent tech CEO could not resist making light of the situation. Elon Musk left a “yikes” emoji in response to an X user who noted that the collapsed crypto exchange FTX had initially also told users their funds were safe amid a wave of losses. Binance co-founder CZ Zhao responded:“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop.” Zhao noted that his SpaceX shares — the product of a Binance-related $500 million investment in Twitter, were now worth more than $1 billion. “Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!”

articles.body: Jio O2 results: Jio Platforms reported a 13.7% year-on-year increase in consolidated net profit to Rs 8,389 crore for the September quarter of FY27, while revenue from operations rose 11.4% to Rs 40,475 crore. The company also recorded growth across key operational parameters, with its customer base expanding to 542.4 million, data traffic increasing 22.1% and average revenue per user (ARPU) rising to Rs 218.8.The results, announced on Friday, mark the company's first earnings announcement since its stock market debut on October 28.Jio Platforms' consolidated net profit increased to Rs 8,389 crore in Q2 FY27 from Rs 7,379 crore in the corresponding quarter last year. Revenue from operations climbed to Rs 40,475 crore from Rs 36,332 crore over the same period.The company also reported an improvement on a sequential basis, with net profit rising 8% from Rs 7,765 crore in the June quarter. Revenue increased 3% quarter-on-quarter.Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) grew 17% year-on-year during the quarter, driven by revenue growth, operating leverage and a 250 basis points expansion in margins.Customer base crosses 542 millionJio Platforms' customer base increased to 542.4 million in the September quarter, compared with 506.4 million in the year-ago period, registering growth of 7.1%.The company added 9.1 million net customers during the quarter, against 8.3 million in Q2 FY26 and 8.9 million in the preceding June quarter.Monthly churn stood at 1.6%, unchanged from the previous quarter but lower than 1.9% recorded in the corresponding period last year, marking a reduction of 30 basis points.For FY26, the reported figures included a customer base of 524.4 million, net customer additions of 36.2 million and monthly churn of 1.7%.Jio ARPU rises to Rs 218.8Jio Platforms' average revenue per user (ARPU) rose to Rs 218.8 in Q2 FY27, up 3.5% from Rs 211.4 in the year-ago quarter. articles.title: ‘They killed us’: Russia’s last independent newspaper falls silent amid pressure from Kremlin
articles.summary: Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper once edited by Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov, one of Russia’s last independent news outlets, announced on Friday they are closing down their it would close down operations due to pressure from authorities.
articles.body: Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s last independent news outlets, announced on Friday it would close down operations due to pressure from authorities. “Novaya Gazeta has been killed,” Editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a video statement. “On November 9, we will turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down our servers and leave…The Russian security services have forced the editorial team to cease operations.” The newspaper, once edited by the Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov, has long been seen as a beacon of Russian investigative reporting. Founded in the early 1990s partially under the patronage of former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, Novaya Gazeta had an adversarial relationship with the Kremlin, but had been under immense pressure from Russian authorities amid a widespread crackdown on the country’s media following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russian lawmakers criminalized the spread of “fake” news that discredits the Russian military in March 2022, forcing scores of journalists including those working at Novaya Gazeta to flee into exile. An offshoot publication, Novaya Gazeta Europe, is based in Riga, Latvia. Sokolov told CNN he believes Novaya Gazeta’s fate reflected the situation in Russian society more broadly which faces a suppressed media landscape. “The information space in Russia has disappeared,” Sokolov said. “People do not know, and have no way of finding out, even what is happening in the neighboring street, because the sources of news available to them are either stories about a Russia that does not exist or propaganda promoting the way of thinking the ruling elite wants to impose on the public.” Novaya Gazeta initially suspended publication of its online and print editions in Russia following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, after receiving a warning from Russia’s media regulator, Roskomnadzor. The move came after Muratov took part, alongside other prominent independent Russian journalists, in an interview with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in March 2022. Novaya Gazeta has a long history of investigating corruption and wrongdoing by various organs of the Russian state. Co-founder Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in October 2021 alongside Philippines journalist Maria Ressa for their “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression.” In April 2022, Muratov said he was attacked with acetone laced red paint while traveling on a train from Moscow to the city of Samara. The newspaper said in a statement that he nearly lost his sight, and the perpetrators were let go. Six of the paper’s journalists have been murdered during its three and a half decades of operation, including Anna Politkovskaya, an ardent critic of President Vladimir Putin who reported extensively on human rights abuses in Chechnya. Politkovskaya was murdered outside her Moscow apartment in 2006, on Putin’s birthday. Muratov and the newspaper itself were labeled “foreign agents.” Russian authorities have increasingly used the label as a way of casting aspersions on the credibility and independence of organizations and people carrying the designation. It’s a sign that the state sees them as associated with foreign influence and carries practical legal implications such as cumbersome financial penalties and reporting requirements. “We carried on as long as we could, but we were evicted from our home and our donations platform that allowed us to receive financial support from our readers has been shut down,” Novaya Gazeta said in a statement published on Friday. “We have been stripped of all our resources. Entirely.” Authorities revoked its license and blocked access to its website inside Russia. Oleg Roldugin, an investigative journalist for the paper was arrested earlier this year for “unlawful access to computerized information,” and the editor-in-chief Sokolov was detained for questioning and his home was searched in connection with the case. In a statement to CNN the paper said, “we cannot continue working under the name ‘Novaya Gazeta.’ ‘Novaya’ no longer exists. One final issue will be published — and that’s it. After that, we’ll take a pause, reflect, and come up with a new life for ourselves.” Muratov has remained a public voice campaigning for release of Russian political prisoners. The Atlantic in September reported on his efforts to lobby for US diplomacy to release jailed Russian dissidents. While critics say such efforts might potentially aid Putin’s bid for sanctions relief, the paper’s former editor and his international stature apparently could not shield the acclaimed newspaper from Russia’s machinery of repression.

articles.title: ExxonMobil and Chevron report blowout profits as Trump touts benefits of high oil prices
articles.summary: The two largest U.S. oil companies, ExxonMobil and Chevron reported blowout profits as oil prices remain sharply elevated due to the U.S. war with Iran.
articles.body: It’s a good time to be an oil company. The two largest U.S. oil companies, ExxonMobil and Chevron, on Friday reported blowout profits that easily beat expectations as oil prices remain sharply elevated because of the U.S. war with Iran. ExxonMobil reported a profit that doubled from the same period last year, while Chevron’s earnings surged more than 180% from a year earlier. As part of the bumper returns, Exxon said it was increasing the dividend it pays to investors. The returns at both companies came as the price of oil surged beyond $100 per barrel and has remained there for months. On Friday, prices accelerated again, with Brent oil trading closing just under $118 per barrel. The highest level that Brent reached since the United States and Israel launched the Iran war in late February was $126, which it is now approaching again. Since the start of the year, Exxon shares have risen 52%, and Chevron shares have returned 50%. Overnight, another major oil company, BP, reported that its profit skyrocketed to an 18-year high. The average price of regular gasoline has soared 40% for consumers since the war broke out. Soaring prices continue to pressure consumers ahead of the midterm elections, where voters have repeatedly said that prices and inflation are primary concerns. In 2024, Donald Trump repeatedly pledged to drive energy costs down. “My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office,” the then-candidate said in September 2024, while adding that it would mean “gasoline below $2 a gallon.” As of Friday, the average gasoline price is currently more than double that. In recent rallies on the campaign trail, the president has celebrated the higher oil and gas profits. “I wonder if I should say this,” Trump mused aloud during a rally Oct. 24, before saying “our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East.” “My people said, ‘Please don’t mention that, sir,’ because people are paying a little higher,” Trump continued. “But what we’ve done for this country, we’re making money like this country has never made before.” “I don’t give a damn: I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune.” The higher prices are also a result of the war between Ukraine and Russia following President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of his neighbor in 2022. “There’s a lot of disruption happening in the world,” ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday morning. “What you’re finding is because of the closure” in the Strait of Hormuz, “shipping has to find new routes around to continue to deliver the products that society desperately needs.” “About half of Russia’s refinery capacity has been taken out from the Ukraine bombing,” he added. “That shortage of refining capacity and availability to the world is what’s driving product prices as high as it is, and frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth,” Woods continued. Since the start of the year, the average nationwide price for diesel fuel has risen 78%. New York-traded diesel futures have soared 130% since the start of the year, likely indicating more price rises could still come at the pump. Both Exxon and Chevron said that they were running their refineries at maximum output to continue making as much diesel as possible. Trump has taken specific note of the impact that diesel could have on the economy. The administration has quickly issued multiple orders and policies in an attempt to bring prices down. The president signed an order allowing more widespread use of an off-road dyed variety of diesel, has pressured European allies to release more of the diesel reserves into the global market, and has announced a deal with Putin for some of that country’s diesel supplies. Trump’s latest move came last week, when he announced $150 million in Defense Production Act funding to “expand petroleum production, storage, and logistics at refineries across.” The moves have not meaningfully brought prices down. On Friday, Woods said his refineries were already being pushed to the limit. “We are at record levels of utilization for our refineries,” he said on CNBC. “If you look at North America, we produce record volumes of diesel. That’s all been a function of trying to drive more product into the marketplace to meet that demand and to drive costs down.”

articles.title: ‘Capacity can’t cope with demand being seen in India:’ SWISS CEO even after adding flights here
articles.summary: BENGALURU: “Capacity can’t cope with the demand being seen in India.” This is what SWISS CEO Jens Fehlinger told TOI in Bengaluru on Wednesday when the
articles.body: BENGALURU: “Capacity can’t cope with the demand being seen in India.” This is what SWISS CEO Jens Fehlinger told TOI in Bengaluru on Wednesday when the airline started flights to the garden city, making it the third Indian city for this Lufthansa group airline after Delhi and Mumbai.The reason: Air India group and IndiGo have significantly cut their long-haul flights to the west primarily due to closure of Pakistan airspace for Indian carriers since last April, even as the demand for international travel to and from the country remains inelastic and high. Once the US-Iran war started on Feb 28, 2026, and all airlines had to cut flights to West Asia, many foreign carriers deployed their spare capacity to India.The Lufthansa group, for instance, used to have 318 monthly flights to India by Lufthansa, SWISS and ITA Airways (erstwhile Alitalia) till Feb 2026. By Aug, that number swelled 9% to 344 and is expected to increase to 383 by Aug 2027.“When we had to temporarily suspend our Dubai flights, we added a second daily service to Delhi (on March 19). Bengaluru, however, had been on our radar for quite some time. We carefully analysed the market, its growth potential and customer demand before deciding to add Bengaluru to our network,” said Fehlinger, a trained pilot who has operated the Airbus A320 and the super jumbo A380 and has been with the Lufthansa group for over two decades now. For the Bengaluru flight, the second daily between Delhi and Zurich has been withdrawn.So why isn’t Bengaluru a daily like Delhi was? “Due to the situation in West Asia, our flights to and from the east take longer routes. Our Tokyo and Shanghai flights now take 1.5 hour and 1 hour longer, respectively. India routes’ flying time is up by 30 minutes. Since Zurich-Bengaluru is a longer route, aircraft rotation takes longer. So we have started with five times a week, which in the next step may become daily,” said the CEO.Will the additional capacity deployed to India be scaled back when West Asia reopens? “We are looking at India for long-term investments and long-term growth. It is the second biggest market for us after the US and our presence here will go only one way — up.”Like all airlines globally, secure aircraft movement, airspace closures and fuel prices and availability are the prime concerns for SWISS in these geopolitically challenged times. “Our routes to the east have become very narrow. There are three routes now, one over the north pole, via Azerbaijan and the third via Saudi Arabia and south India. The rest is closed basically,” he said.While the cash-rich group does fuel hedging, it is preparing for fuel supply shocks despite seeing little chance of that happening. “At the moment there is no foreseeable fuel shortage at our home hubs. We are well supplied in Geneva and Zurich with pipelines and trains. But we are prepared for every scenario. If fuel (supply) stops in between, we could do tankering where we fill up at an, airport (for short hauls) that has fuel and fly back home and out without refuelling there. Or we could have fuel stops for long hauls. As of now, we don’t see the same will need to be done but we started preparations for all fuel supply scenarios from March itself. No one knows what the next few months will be like,” he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol: 'The turn has occurred' — now it's in growth mode
articles.summary: The comeback at Starbucks has morphed into something more lasting.
articles.body:
The turnaround at Starbucks ( SBUX ) has been served up, and now it looks to be a caffeinated period of growth.

"I think we're back to being just a growth company. I think the turn has occurred. And now we have all these growth opportunities in front of us because we've got a strong foundation," Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said on Sozzi Unleashed .

Starbucks delivered a bottom-line beat in its fiscal fourth quarter results on Thursday evening, posting adjusted earnings of $0.80 per share versus estimates for $0.71.

Three highlights in particular stood out, in addition to the earnings beat.

Global comparable-store sales jumped 7.2%, and US same-store sales accelerated to 7.7%, driven by healthy ticket and transaction expansion. The company reiterated strength in cold beverages and food.

Sales strength led to a 460 basis point expansion in the operating margin to 14%.

Starbucks also offered initial fiscal 2027 adjusted profit guidance of $3.15 to $3.25 per share, ahead of the $3.14 estimate.

Niccol said the company is full speed ahead on revamping its drive-thrus to unleash the power of AI, offering more caffeine-free afternoon beverages (think drinks with collagen) and new portable foods to match.

"After a strong quarter that showcased significant margin improvement and continued momentum on top-line, we believe Starbucks has raised the bar for excellence," Bernstein analyst Danilo Gargiulo said.

articles.title: Gold hits one-year low, silver slips below $50 as inflation fears bite
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Precious metals are having a rough run, with the latest sell-off taking gold to a one-year low and pushing silver below the $50-an-ounce mark
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Precious metals are having a rough run, with the latest sell-off taking gold to a one-year low and pushing silver below the $50-an-ounce mark for the first time since almost a year.Rising energy prices and stubborn inflation concerns are weighing on investor sentiment, with expectations growing that US interest rates could stay higher for longer. Both metals extended their monthly losses on Friday, with silver taking a sharper hit.Gold continued its downward journey on Friday, with spot prices falling 2.7% to $3,910.53 per ounce. This was the metal's lowest level since October 2025. US gold futures for December delivery also slipped 2.8% to $3,919.60 per ounce.Bullion prices have declined 5.9% so far this month and are on track to record their second consecutive monthly fall.Silver fared worse, with spot prices dropping 5.8% to $49.34 per ounce. The decline took the metal below the $50 mark for the first time since November 2025, bringing it to its lowest level since that month.Why are precious metal prices falling?The prospect of interest rates staying elevated for longer is putting pressure on precious metals. Higher energy prices have added to inflation concerns, prompting central banks to maintain a cautious stance on monetary policy.Major central banks kept interest rates unchanged this week, but their indications suggested that the tightening cycle may not be over. The US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank both flagged inflation risks stemming from surging energy costs."Ongoing concerns about inflation have multiple central banks continuing to tilt hawkish," said Peter Grant, vice president and senior metals strategist at Zaner Metals."Even though holds were delivered by major central banks this week, the indication was that the higher-for-longer theme prevails, and that's weighing on precious metals."US inflation data released on Thursday further strengthened these concerns. Inflation accelerated in September as consumers paid more for gasoline and other goods, bolstering economists' expectations of an interest rate hike in December.Tech stock sell-off adds to precious metals pressureThe sharp decline in technology stocks may have added to the pressure on precious metals, with analysts at Commerzbank pointing to the possibility of forced selling and margin calls following the tech stock sell-off.However, the analysts believe the fall in precious metal prices has been excessive and expect a recovery."We consider the fall in precious metal prices to be exaggerated and continue to expect a recovery," they added.The tech-heavy Nasdaq was also poised for steep losses at Friday's opening as concerns over artificial intelligence spending weighed on technology stocks.Meanwhile, oil prices continued to climb and were headed for a fourth consecutive monthly gain. Rising energy costs have strengthened expectations of interest rates remaining elevated for an extended period, making non-yielding assets such as gold less attractive.Asian gold demand remains subduedWeak physical demand in key Asian markets has added to the challenges facing gold.Back at home, buyers held back from making purchases this week, expecting prices to decline further.Meanwhile, demand in China, the top gold-consuming country, also remained muted, offering little support to the market.The sell-off extended to other precious metals as well. Platinum prices dropped 4% to $1,428.35 per ounce, their lowest level since September 2025.Palladium fell 3.1% to $975.25 per ounce, touching its lowest level since June 2025. Both metals were poised to register declines for the week as well as the month.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: What Binance users should do right now following $6.3 billion hack
articles.summary: A $6.3 billion security breach has shaken Binance. Here's what users should know and do to protect their accounts.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, said on Oct. 29 that a security incident affected $6.3 billion in customer assets, which would be the largest crypto hack ever. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who stepped down as CEO in 2023, said the theft "does look like a hack."

Binance has temporarily suspended all withdrawals and deposits and said it would cover all losses of an estimated $6.3 billion in digital assets using its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company reserves.

"Your assets are safe," Richard Teng, Binance co-CEO, said in a video statement on X , noting that stolen assets were in the process of being recovered.

Yi He, Binance co-founder and co-CEO, said that customer withdrawals should resume by Sunday in a post on X .

Tomas Sinicki, managing director at Coveron, an identity theft and scam protection service developed by Nord Security, offers this advice for crypto holders:

Never keep more on an exchange than you need for trading . Even the largest platforms can freeze withdrawals overnight, as Binance users just discovered. Long-term holdings belong in a wallet where you control the keys, as an exchange account is ultimately in someone else's hands.

Be skeptical of urgency, especially during market panic . Incidents like this are prime time for follow-up scams: fake "exchange support" messages and phishing emails promising to help recover funds.

Limit what a single compromise can unlock . Use unique passwords, enable multifactor authentication, and regularly revoke permissions for apps and services you no longer use — so one breached account or device cannot cascade into everything else.

Know what of yours is already exposed . Credentials and personal data from past breaches circulate on the dark web, and crypto holders are high-value targets. Continuous monitoring tells you what is out there before an attacker uses it.

Act fast on alerts . In fast-moving incidents, speed determines how much can be contained. The same is true for individuals: The sooner you respond to a breach or fraud alert, the more you can limit the fallout.

Binance advised customers to "rely only on official Binance channels for updates" and to contact Binance customer support with any further questions.

Sinicki says that the full details of the incident aren't known yet and may not be fully disclosed for some time.

"Even what is confirmed so far points to a familiar pattern," Sinicki said in a statement. "If reports are accurate, attackers compromised a single employee's laptop and used the legitimate access it held. That should tell every organization where the real perimeter now sits. Criminals no longer break in, they log in."

On X, Binance said, "Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified."

Binance has said it will reimburse customers, but Sinicki cautions that much is still unknown.

"Much of this story is still uncertain: the final losses, the number of breach points, even who is responsible," Sinicki said. "That uncertainty is itself the lesson: by the time the facts are settled, the damage is done. Binance can freeze assets and promise to cover losses because it has billions in reserve and traceable transactions."

Teng, Binance co-CEO said on X , "We never use any customer funds, so they are not impacted. What was affected in this incident was Binance's own hot wallet. User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture. The vast majority sits in cold wallets, and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes a withdrawal."

Taking preventative measures with your digital investments

Bryan Courchesne, founder and CEO of DAiM, a wealth management firm specializing in crypto, says incidents like this should remind investors that security and custody design matter, especially as digital-asset markets mature and attract more sophisticated adversaries.

"At the same time, the industry has repeatedly shown an ability to contain damage, make users whole, and continue growing. Licensed platforms with strong cold-storage practices and transparent reserves have a solid track record, and the long-term case for Bitcoin as a scarce digital asset remains intact," Courchesne said. "Markets have digested similar events before and ultimately moved higher."

Courchesne said crypto investors should:

Rely only on official communications from the platform (app, verified email, or website).

Review personal account security: Use strong unique passwords, hardware-based 2FA where possible, and limited device access.

For material long-term holdings, evaluate whether a regulated, qualified custodian or professionally managed structure with transparent cold-storage practices better fits their needs.

Maintain a long-term perspective. Past exchange incidents that were properly contained and made whole have not derailed the broader Bitcoin adoption thesis.

Panic-sell core holdings or move assets in haste to unverified destinations.

Click on links in unsolicited emails, texts, or social messages claiming to "help" recover funds or "secure" accounts — phishing spikes after these events.

Share seed phrases, private keys, or remote-access credentials with anyone.

Ignore basic operational hygiene (device security, access controls, and understanding where the majority of assets actually sit).

articles.title: Burger King's chicken nuggets just got a Whopper-like makeover — fries are next
articles.summary: The turnaround at Burger King continues to sizzle.
articles.body:
The turnaround at Burger King in the US continues to sizzle.

Burger King's US comparable sales increased a stunning 8.4% in the third quarter, parent company Restaurant Brands International ( QSR ) said in its third quarter earnings release this week.

"I think people still look at fast food as a treat, and they want to treat themselves once in a while, and when they want to treat themselves, they don't want to compromise. They don't want to say, 'Well, I'm going to go get the cheap meal. Or the least expensive product, or the lowest-quality product.' They want to feel like they are treating themselves and they're being treated well. So, when you're talking about elevation and improving your products at a time where they're struggling, it's like that's their reward," Burger King US president Tom Curtis said on Sozzi Unleashed .

The sales strength at Burger King — almost unseen in the wider fast food scene — could be directly tied back to the chain's operational improvements under Curtis.

BK recently reintroduced its chicken nuggets following guest feedback, offering improved breading and a juicier nugget. Curtis is locked in on fries next.

"I think [fries are] a very passionate topic for consumers. So we'll do something with fries. Not sure exactly what and when yet, but it takes a while to figure all of it out," Curtis said.

This is on the heels of Burger King making several subtle but meaningful changes to its Whopper for the first time in nearly a decade.

The updated burger now features a more premium, better-tasting bun and a reformulated, creamier mayonnaise. Toppings like lettuce, tomatoes, onions, and pickles are prepared to taste fresher and stack more neatly.

Another major change is the packaging: Instead of being wrapped in paper, the burger is now served in a box to prevent it from getting squished and to maintain its presentation.

The company has marketed all of these improvements to consumers with Curtis serving as the frontman.

Curtis released a TikTok video earlier this year in which he took an enthusiastic bite of a Whopper — in response to a viral moment by the CEO of McDonald's — and joked that the only thing missing is a napkin. He also gave out his phone number so people could share what they thought about the brand.

Curtis ended up talking to 1,500 people and getting tens of thousands more messages. He has poured these findings back into his operational improvements for Burger King.

"The brand could capitalize on the increased consideration (from 70% to 78%), further menu elevation and remodels, that generate meaningful sales uplift. The challenge appears to be sequencing these opportunities effectively, rather than finding new growth levers," Bernstein analyst Danilo Gargiulo wrote.

articles.summary: Zensar Technologies Q2 revenue rose 2% YoY (4.1% QoQ) as AI-led deals made up 36% of the order book; EBIT margin dipped to 13.4%.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Mid-sized IT services firm Zensar Technologies reported a 2% year-on-year increase in revenue in constant currency terms, while sequential growth stood at 4.1%. in the September quarter. Its EBIT margin stood at 13.4%, down 30 basis points year-on-year.Banking and financial services was a key growth driver, with revenue in the vertical rising 17.1% year-on-year and 7.1% sequentially in constant currency terms. The US business grew 2.5% year-on-year, while Africa expanded 2.2%. Healthcare and life sciences declined 9.9%, and telecom, media and technology contracted 21.6% year-on-year in constant currency terms.AI-influenced deals accounted for 36% of the company’s order book in the quarter. CEO and managing director Manish Tandon said the company was seeing broad-based growth across verticals, except telecom. He said companies continuing to sell traditional services in traditional ways would find the market diminishing, while those taking newer offerings and concept-led solutions to customers would find opportunities.Tandon said around $30 million of deals were awaiting paperwork before being added to the order book, and he was not particularly concerned about the delay.On client expectations of productivity gains, he said IT services companies would increasingly have to move from time-and-materials contracts to outcome- and output-based models.He also believes AI is changing the industry’s talent requirements. “Writing code has become a commodity,” Tandon said, adding that companies would need engineers with deeper software engineering skills who could instruct AI tools to generate code, rather than those who merely write code quickly.Zensar’s headcount increased to 12,320, with 978 net additions during the quarter.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hold the rate. The Fed can’t pump oil.
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve opted to maintain interest rates between 3.75 percent and 4 percent during its recent meeting, a decision supported by analysis suggesting that recent inflation was primarily driven by energy costs rather than widespread economic pressure.
articles.body:
At its recent meeting, the Federal Reserve decided to maintain its interest rate target , forgoing a hike that would have been the second in six weeks. The target federal funds rate remained between 3.75 percent and 4 percent, with two members of the Federal Open Market Committee dissenting.

The Fed should be commended for its decision. While some may argue that recent inflation justified a rate hike, the increase in aggregate prices was almost entirely predicated on energy cost increases. The fact is that no central bank on earth has ever lowered the price of a barrel of crude by raising the cost of a home equity line of credit.

Consumer prices are up 3.7 percent over the past year. Energy is up 20 percent and gasoline 34 percent. Energy alone accounts for about 1.4 points of that 3.7 — around the same as housing, which normally drives the index and carries more than a third of its weight. When the energy shock is stripped out, the inflation picture changes dramatically.

Economists, and indeed the Fed, know that energy is the most volatile component, which is why they point to core inflation, the index that leaves out food and energy prices. However, even that might not provide the full picture of just how much oil price changes permeate the entire economy.

The issue is that core removes prices by category, not by what drives them. Despite jet fuel being one of the highest costs an airline pays, airline fares are counted within core; fares are up 22 percent over the year . So are the trucking and delivery charges baked into the price of nearly everything in shopping malls.

Reaching a better methodology would require asking this: What would inflation have been if energy and the goods and services that are most energy intensive had risen at a normal 2 percent rate while measuring the realized prices of everything else?

Using the Labor Department’s own weights for the Consumer Price Index (CPI), the answer is 2.1 percent over the past year and about 2.5 percent over the past three months. Month by month, even as crude oil rose from the low $80s to above $100, this measure was 0.20, 0.22, and 0.21 percent, respectively.

If we apply the same methodology to the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, the Fed’s preferred method of measuring inflation, that figure is still at 2.6 percent year over year. This includes the latest September Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index data that was released on Oct. 29, the day after the Fed meeting, further reinforcing that the Fed made the right choice.

The Fed’s own regional banks also reach the same conclusion through a different calculation. The Dallas Fed’s “trimmed mean” measure, which discards the largest price swings each month, fell to 2.2 percent in August, its lowest reading of the year. The Cleveland Fed’s median price index was at 2.6 percent in September. Every one of these methods says that inflation is within a point of the target.

In August, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh argued at Jackson Hole that inflation is “widespread” because more than half of the 199 categories in the government’s price index rose faster than 3 percent. The problem with this framing is that it equally weighs all goods categories, regardless of how much of a family’s budget each constitutes.

The above measures show that when one accounts for what portion of household budgets go to various items, inflation is not widespread; it is instead largely limited to oil-dependent items. In these circumstances, there was little justification to reach for a blunt instrument whose costs fall on the entire economy.

An October hike would have put unwarranted pressure on Americans. Families would have faced higher payments on car loans and credit cards. Small businesses would have paid more to borrow. Not to mention the fact that the effects of an interest rate change take a year or more to fully suffuse through the economy, meaning the full effects of a hike would have persisted far longer than the current energy shock.

The Fed was right to hold rates in October, and moving forward, they should also give greater weight to measures that account for the kind of narrow price shocks that we see today. Whether it’s the “trimmed mean” or holding energy-intensive goods to 2 percent, the public deserves to know what specifically is driving price changes, which in turn also provides them with greater clarity on long-run trends.

Warsh also indicated that some future meetings would focus on monetary policy strategy, not just rate setting. This bodes well for taking seriously the reports from the taskforces he created upon taking office, particularly the two looking at improving the data the Fed uses to make policy and the appropriate size of the Fed’s balance sheet.

Interest rates are a powerful lever but must be targeted towards inflation pressures that are responsive to interest rate changes. Higher rates do not correct for an energy shock derived from a war in the Middle East.

Michael Faulkender is co-chair, Economy and Trade Policy; chair, AI and Emerging Technology Policy at AFPI and former deputy secretary of the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Jeff Schlagenhauf is director of Economy and Trade Policy at AFPI.

articles.title: Google loses $500bn as China stocks suffer worst rout since 2016: What's happening to global AI?
articles.summary: For the past few years, artificial intelligence has been Wall Street's favourite investment story.
articles.body: For the past few years, artificial intelligence has been Wall Street's favourite investment story. Pour billions into chips, build data centres, promise a revolution and watch valuations soar. But the mood music is changing. Investors are beginning to ask an increasingly uncomfortable question: When, exactly, will all this spending start paying off?The answer is becoming more important as some of the biggest names in technology face a bruising week. Google's parent Alphabet suffered a record one-day fall, wiping more than $500 billion off its market value. Intel's shares plunged on a weak outlook, Amazon came under pressure over its spending and sales forecasts, while China's blue-chip stocks recorded their steepest monthly decline in more than a decade.From Silicon Valley to Shanghai, the AI trade is running into a reality check. So what's happening?The bill is getting bigger, but where are the returns?Alphabet became the latest casualty after its third-quarter results disappointed investors. Its shares fell more than 12% on Thursday, their worst single-day percentage decline on record, wiping roughly $500 billion off its market capitalisation. The company's market value dropped from around $3.97 trillion to $3.46 trillion.The concerns went beyond a quarterly earnings miss. Alphabet reported revenue growth of 25% to $127.6 billion, but its advertising business failed to meet expectations. More significantly, executives acknowledged that Google's AI Mode was generating lower advertising monetisation than traditional search queries.Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetisation being seen. That admission raised a difficult question: Could Google's attempt to reinvent search with AI end up undermining the advertising business that finances much of its empire?The pressure is compounded by spending. Alphabet recorded $51.4 billion in capital expenditure in the third quarter alone and reported a second consecutive quarter of negative free cash flow. Microsoft, by comparison, generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow during the quarter despite its AI investments.Amazon has also faced scrutiny. Its shares fell after it offered a cautious sales forecast for the crucial holiday quarter. The company reported negative cash flow of $42 billion, reflecting the scale of its spending. Chief executive Andy Jassy defended the investment, arguing that cloud services, retail and its own chips could unlock enormous future opportunities.Microsoft has fared relatively better. Revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion, while its cloud business grew 30% to $63 billion. Its results offered investors evidence that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, even as questions persist over where the technology's long-term value will ultimately accrue.From chipmakers to China, the sell-off spreadsIntel shares plunged more than 25% in premarket trading on Friday after the chipmaker forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion-$16 billion, below analysts' expectations of $17.07 billion. Its finance chief also said the company did not expect positive cash flow this year.The warning dragged semiconductor stocks lower, including Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm and Broadcom. Server makers Dell, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Super Micro Computer also fell, showing how the sell-off is spreading across the AI infrastructure supply chain.China's markets have taken an even harder hit. The CSI300 index fell 8.5% in October, its biggest monthly decline since early 2016, while the technology-focused STAR50 has lost around 40% in less than four months, according to Reuters. The correction has erased roughly $480 billion in market value from Chinese AI and semiconductor leaders.Chinese technology stocks had surged on expectations of strong domestic AI demand and Beijing's push for technological self-reliance. But high valuations, concerns over export restrictions and questions about future demand have undermined the rally. Some popular stocks, including robotics and chipmaking companies, have lost around half their value.The correction also highlights how heavily AI has come to dominate China's markets. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related stocks account for 42% of market capitalisation and 57% of turnover across mainland-listed and Hong Kong-listed shares. Investors are asking who can afford the AI raceThe scale of the investment explains the growing nervousness. Morgan Stanley expects spending on AI infrastructure to exceed $1 trillion next year. JP Morgan estimates global AI capital expenditure could reach $5.5 trillion by 2030, with $900 billion spent in 2026 alone.Companies are increasingly turning to debt markets to finance the build-out. Meta, Amazon and Alphabet have issued substantial amounts of bonds in recent years, while Microsoft is reportedly planning a $25 billion US investment-grade bond sale. Rising borrowing costs could make this strategy more expensive, particularly if AI revenues fail to keep pace.Investors are already reassessing their exposure. US equity funds recorded net outflows of $6.65 billion in the week ended October 28, their first weekly withdrawals in three weeks, according to LSEG Lipper data.You use AI every day.
